title: The Great Depression
in30Seconds: The Great Depression was the deepest economic collapse of the modern industrial age. It began with the U.S. stock market crash of October 1929 and lasted through the 1930s. At its worst, in 1933, nearly a quarter of American workers had no job, banks failed, and drought turned Great Plains farms into the Dust Bowl. President Franklin Roosevelt answered with the New Deal, whose effectiveness historians still debate. Full recovery arrived only with World War II mobilization in 1941.
whyItMatters: The Great Depression reshaped how governments and citizens think about the economy. It produced institutions Americans still rely on, including federal deposit insurance, securities regulation, and Social Security, and it made steady employment a central test of government. Studying it teaches a core historical skill: separating a dramatic trigger, the 1929 crash, from the deeper structural causes that economists weigh differently, and separating established facts from the genuine debate over how well the New Deal worked. Those habits of careful causal reasoning apply to every later economic crisis, including the 2008 recession, and to arguments about the proper role of government today.
learningObjectives: Define the Great Depression and identify when it began and ended.
Distinguish the 1929 stock market crash as a trigger from the deeper causes economists cite.
Explain the human toll, including mass unemployment, bank failures, and the Dust Bowl.
Describe the New Deal's main relief, recovery, and reform programs.
Analyze the historical debate over the New Deal's effectiveness and how the Depression finally ended.

collegeVersion.heading: The crash of 1929
collegeVersion.body: The Great Depression is usually dated from the stock market crash of October 1929. Through the 1920s, stock prices had climbed on a wave of speculation. Many buyers purchased shares 'on margin,' meaning they put down only a small fraction of the price and borrowed the rest, planning to sell at a profit before the balance came due. This works only while prices keep rising. When confidence broke, the fall was violent. On 'Black Thursday,' October 24, 1929, the New York Stock Exchange lost about 11 percent of its value; on 'Black Tuesday,' October 29, holders traded more than sixteen million shares and lost over $14 billion in a single day. By the end of the fall the market had lost almost half its value. It is important, though, to see the crash as a trigger rather than the whole story. Only about 10 percent of American households owned stock. What turned a market panic into a decade-long depression was that more than 90 percent of banks had themselves invested in the market, so when stocks collapsed, banks failed, credit froze, and the damage spread far beyond investors.

collegeVersion.heading: Why the economy collapsed
collegeVersion.body: Economists and historians agree on the list of contributing causes but weigh them differently, and that disagreement is itself worth understanding. A speculative bubble and margin buying left the financial system fragile. A wave of bank failures destroyed savings and sharply contracted the money supply: Federal Reserve History reports that from the fall of 1930 through the winter of 1933 the money supply fell by nearly 30 percent, producing severe deflation that deepened every debt. Some economists, notably Milton Friedman and later Ben Bernanke, argue that the Federal Reserve's failure to stop this contraction was a decisive error; Bernanke publicly acknowledged in 2002 that the Fed's mistakes contributed to the disaster. Other explanations emphasize overproduction and underconsumption, in which factories and farms produced more than a public with stagnant or unequal incomes could buy, and deep inequality in the distribution of wealth. Still others stress international factors: World War I war debts and reparations, the rigidities of the international gold standard, and high tariffs that choked global trade. No single cause explains the Depression, and part of learning the topic is holding several causes in mind at once.

collegeVersion.heading: The human toll and the Dust Bowl
collegeVersion.body: The suffering was staggering and uneven. According to the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library, at the height of the Depression in 1933 about 24.9 percent of the total workforce, roughly 12.83 million people, was unemployed. Within the first year alone U.S. gross national product had already fallen by more than 25 percent, and unemployment tripled from 1.5 million at the end of 1929 to 4.5 million. Bank failures wiped out the savings of families who had done nothing wrong. Homeless people built shantytowns that critics mockingly called 'Hoovervilles,' after President Herbert Hoover, and breadlines became a defining image of the era. In the Great Plains, years of overplowing and overuse of the land met a severe drought to produce the Dust Bowl: enormous dust storms that buried fields and homes. Ruined farm families, many nicknamed 'Okies,' loaded their belongings and drove west looking for work, a migration John Steinbeck made famous in The Grapes of Wrath. Even late in the decade, rural poverty remained widespread.

collegeVersion.heading: The New Deal
collegeVersion.body: Franklin D. Roosevelt took office in March 1933 at the very bottom of the crisis, when the banking system had collapsed. Within forty-eight hours he declared a national bank holiday, and Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act. Roosevelt then launched a broad program he grouped under three words: relief for people in immediate need, recovery for the economy, and reform to prevent a repeat. Relief and jobs came through agencies such as the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC, 1933), which put young men to work on conservation projects, and the Works Progress Administration (WPA, 1935), which eventually employed more than eight million people building roads, schools, and public art. Reform reshaped finance: the Glass-Steagall Banking Act of 1933 separated commercial from investment banking and created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to insure ordinary deposits, and federal securities laws of 1933 and 1934 created the Securities and Exchange Commission to police the markets. The Social Security Act of 1935 built a permanent safety net of old-age pensions and unemployment insurance. Much of this framework still governs American life.

collegeVersion.heading: The debate and the end
collegeVersion.body: Whether the New Deal 'worked' is a genuine and continuing debate, and a careful student presents it even-handedly rather than picking a side. Supporters point out that it delivered urgent relief, restored confidence in the banks, and created durable institutions, and that unemployment fell substantially from its 1933 peak. Critics at the time attacked it from both directions: conservatives warned that federal spending and power were growing dangerously, while some on the left argued it did too little for the poorest Americans, for women, and for African Americans, who were often excluded from its benefits. Economically, recovery was real but incomplete. A sharp 'double-dip' recession in 1937 and 1938, partly blamed on the government tightening policy too soon, showed how fragile the rebound was. On the timing of full recovery there is broad agreement: as Federal Reserve History and the Roosevelt Library both note, return to full output and employment came only with mobilization for World War II. After 1941, military drafts and defense production finally absorbed the unemployed, ending the Depression.

vocabulary.definition: The severe worldwide economic downturn of the 1930s, centered on the United States, beginning in 1929 and lasting until World War II mobilization in 1941.
Purchasing stock with a small down payment and borrowed money, planning to sell at a higher price before the balance is due; profitable only while prices keep rising.
The sudden collapse of U.S. stock prices in October 1929, marked by Black Thursday (Oct. 24) and Black Tuesday (Oct. 29), treated as the Depression's trigger.
A sustained fall in the general level of prices; in the 1930s it raised the real burden of debts and discouraged spending.
The total amount of money and readily spendable funds in an economy; it contracted by nearly 30 percent between 1930 and 1933.
The 1930s ecological disaster in which overfarming and drought produced massive dust storms across the Great Plains, driving families to migrate.
Franklin D. Roosevelt's program of federal relief, recovery, and reform launched in 1933 to combat the Depression.
The three goals organizing the New Deal: immediate aid to people, restoring the economy, and long-term changes to prevent another collapse.
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, created by the Glass-Steagall Act of 1933 to insure bank deposits and restore confidence in banks.
The 1935 law that created a national system of old-age pensions and unemployment insurance, a lasting part of the U.S. safety net.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: In the 1920s lots of people borrowed money to buy pieces of companies called stocks, betting the prices would keep going up. In 1929 the prices suddenly crashed, and the people who had borrowed could not pay it back. Banks lost money too, so they closed, and when a bank closed the savings inside it vanished. With no money, businesses stopped hiring, and about one in four grown-ups who wanted a job could not find one. On top of that, huge dust storms destroyed farms in the middle of the country. The government, led by President Roosevelt, created new programs that gave people jobs, protected the money in banks, and started Social Security. Things got better slowly, but the country did not fully recover until it geared up its factories for World War II.
eli10.analogy: Imagine a game of musical chairs where players keep borrowing chairs to look richer. As long as the music plays and everyone believes, it seems fine. When the music stops in 1929, everyone grabs at once, there are nowhere near enough real chairs, and the players who borrowed owe chairs they never truly had, so the whole game collapses.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy captures the sudden loss of confidence and the danger of borrowed money, but a real economy is not a fixed number of chairs. Governments can add 'chairs' by changing the money supply and spending, which is exactly what the debate over the Federal Reserve and the New Deal is about, and a depression drags on for years rather than ending in one round.

workedExample: Trace the chain of causation for one family. In 1928 a shopkeeper buys $1,000 of stock but pays only $100 down, borrowing $900 on margin, confident prices will rise. In October 1929 the market loses nearly half its value; his broker demands the $900 he owes, which he does not have, so he is wiped out. His bank, which also invested depositors' money in stocks, cannot cover withdrawals and fails, erasing his savings account too. With no credit and frightened customers, his shop's sales collapse and he lays off his one employee, adding to the millions unemployed. Multiply this single chain across the country and you can see why a crash affecting only the roughly 10 percent of households that owned stock could still push nearly 25 percent of all workers out of a job by 1933.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing the 1929 stock market crash single-handedly caused the Great Depression.
commonMistakes.correction: The crash was the trigger, but only about 10 percent of households owned stock. The Depression deepened because banks failed, the money supply contracted, and demand collapsed; economists weigh these underlying causes differently.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the New Deal quickly ended the Depression.
commonMistakes.correction: The New Deal provided relief and lasting reforms and lowered unemployment from its 1933 peak, but recovery was incomplete. A 1937-38 recession set it back, and full employment returned only with World War II mobilization in 1941.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating 'the New Deal worked' or 'the New Deal failed' as settled fact.
commonMistakes.correction: Its effectiveness is a real historical and economic debate. State the established facts, then present both the supporters' case and the critics' case from left and right without declaring a winner.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing the Dust Bowl with the financial crisis.
commonMistakes.correction: The Dust Bowl was a separate ecological disaster caused by overfarming and drought on the Great Plains. It worsened the human toll and drove migration, but it was not the cause of the stock market crash or bank failures.

commonMistakes.mistake: Citing the 25 percent unemployment figure as an exact, universally agreed number.
commonMistakes.correction: The FDR Presidential Library gives 24.9 percent for the 1933 peak; because official unemployment surveys did not yet exist, such Depression-era figures are careful historical estimates. Attribute and date the number rather than stating it as a precise fact.

compareContrast.distinction: The crash was the dramatic event that started the slide; the underlying causes (bank failures, a shrinking money supply, overproduction, inequality, and international strains) determined how deep and long the Depression became.

The First New Deal focused on emergency banking relief and recovery agencies like the CCC; the Second New Deal added the WPA and the Social Security Act, building a longer-term safety net and answering critics.
Relief and recovery (CCC, WPA) aimed to help people and restart the economy right away; reform (FDIC, SEC, Social Security) changed the rules permanently to prevent a future collapse.

keyTakeaway: The Great Depression began with the 1929 stock market crash but was driven by deeper failures in banking, the money supply, and demand; it caused mass unemployment (about 24.9 percent in 1933) and the Dust Bowl, prompted Roosevelt's New Deal of relief, recovery, and reform, and ended only with World War II mobilization in 1941, while the New Deal's effectiveness remains debated.

questionBank.prompt: The stock market crash usually treated as the trigger of the Great Depression occurred in which month and year?
questionBank.explanation: The crash came in October 1929, with Black Thursday on October 24 and Black Tuesday on October 29. March 1933 was the low point of the Depression and Roosevelt's inauguration; December 1941 marks U.S. entry into World War II, which helped end it; 1919 is a decade too early.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the date of the 1929 stock market crash

questionBank.prompt: In the 1920s stock market, what did it mean to buy stock 'on margin'?
options: Buying stock only with cash a person had fully saved in advance
Buying stock issued directly by the federal government
Buying household goods on store credit rather than stock
Buying stock with a small down payment and borrowed money, intending to sell before the balance was due
questionBank.explanation: Margin buying meant putting down only a fraction of the price and borrowing the rest, betting on selling at a profit first. It only works while prices rise, which made the system fragile. The other options describe cash purchases, government issuance, or ordinary consumer credit, none of which is margin buying.
questionBank.skill: Explaining the mechanics of buying on margin

questionBank.prompt: According to the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library, roughly what share of the U.S. workforce was unemployed at the 1933 peak of the Depression?
questionBank.explanation: The FDR Library gives 24.9 percent, about 12.83 million people, for the 1933 peak, commonly rounded to about one in four workers. About 5 percent reflects a healthy economy; 10 percent matches the early spike, not the peak; 50 percent overstates it.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the attributed peak unemployment figure

questionBank.prompt: A town remembers a New Deal program that hired unemployed young men to plant trees, fight erosion, and build park trails. Which program does this describe?
questionBank.explanation: The CCC (1933) put young men to work on conservation projects, exactly the kind of work described. The FDIC insures bank deposits, the SEC regulates securities markets, and Social Security provides pensions and unemployment insurance; none of those is a conservation work program.
questionBank.skill: Matching a New Deal work program to its function

questionBank.prompt: Historians and economists debate the New Deal's effectiveness. Which statement best reflects the widely accepted view of when the Depression fully ended?
options: The 1929 crash caused an immediate but brief downturn that ended by 1931
The First New Deal restored full employment by the end of 1934
Full recovery in output and employment came with mobilization for World War II around 1941
The economy never recovered and stayed in depression through the 1950s
questionBank.explanation: Both Federal Reserve History and the FDR Library note that full output and employment returned only with World War II mobilization around 1941; a 1937-38 recession shows the New Deal recovery was incomplete. The Depression lasted far more than two years, the New Deal did not restore full employment by 1934, and recovery clearly arrived well before the 1950s.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing the timing of recovery and the New Deal debate

provenance.rightsStatus: reference-only sources (OpenStax CC BY, Federal Reserve History, FDR Presidential Library); no source prose adapted
provenance.transformation: Facts, dates, and figures verified against OpenStax U.S. History, Federal Reserve History, and the FDR Presidential Library; all prose is original. Key figures (24.9% 1933 unemployment; ~30% money-supply contraction) are attributed and dated, and the New Deal-effectiveness question and weighting of causes are presented as open debates.
